metadata.file_name: 113. Tyack et al. (2024). Using convolutional neural networks to automatically score eight TIMSS 2019 graphical response items.pdf
metadata.title: Using convolutional neural networks to automatically score eight TIMSS 2019 graphical response items

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items (eight items across Grade 4 and Grade 8) with student responses collected from participating countries. The analytic sample is constructed per item by taking screenshot-based image responses, converting them to greyscale, resizing to fixed pixel dimensions, and mapping human rater scores to integer labels (incorrect/partial/full). The paper does not report applying TIMSS complex survey weights (e.g., student sampling weights) or replicate-weight procedures; instead, it trains CNN classifiers using keras and evaluates performance via hold-out splits and five-fold cross-validation. Because the modeling is ML-based image classification and the manuscript does not describe weight-aware estimation, the analysis is treated as unweighted, and results should be interpreted as validation of scoring agreement rather than population-representative achievement estimation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are CNN classifications of image responses into human rater score categories (binary or trichotomous), not PV-based achievement scores. The manuscript describes IRT-based expected scores (ES) used for an IRT-informed data-cleaning/sample-assignment stage, but it does not document any missing-data strategy for questionnaire/context variables or for the image-response dataset (e.g., how incomplete images or missing labels were handled). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling in the ML pipeline.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response items: identified all graphical response items in TIMSS 2019, excluded the “Building” PSI item already modeled by von Davier et al. (2022), and then selected eight eligible items (five Grade 4 and three Grade 8; one Grade 8 item is trichotomous). For each item, responses were collected from countries that participated in eTIMSS 2019, then pre-processed into fixed-size greyscale image arrays (target sizes 64x64 or 75x75). For data cleaning, responses were split into training/validation sets using stratified random sampling by country and score category; CNN misclassifications were manually reviewed and responses identified as incorrectly or inconsistently scored by human raters were removed from the final modeling dataset. For the trichotomous item ME62300, training data were augmented to increase representation of partial-credit responses.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 Mathematics (graphical response items; dichotomous scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: CNN-scored item category agreement with human raters (incorrect vs correct/partial)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Best CNNs: average accuracy 99.37%–99.92% across seven dichotomous items; F1-scores between 0.9948 and 0.9992; losses reported as low (e.g., 0.0063–0.0298 average loss across items in Table 8).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 4 graphical response item the study leveraged convolutional neural networks to classify each student image into the same score categories as human raters, finding that the CNNs achieved near-perfect agreement (≈99% accuracy and F1 ≥ 0.9948) for dichotomous items. This indicates that CNN-based automated scoring can serve as a reliable second scoring channel for graphical constructed-response items, potentially reducing rater workload while improving consistency checks, though the study validates agreement rather than causal effects on achievement.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 Mathematics (graphical response items; trichotomous scoring)
main_findings.target_variable: CNN-scored item category agreement with human raters (incorrect vs partial vs full credit)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Trichotomous item ME62300: accuracy 97.99% and average F1-score 0.9766 on the clean validation sample (Table 8); average loss 0.1214; for incorrectly human-scored responses, accuracy 88.81% (Table 9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS Grade 8 graphical response item the study leveraged convolutional neural networks to classify each student image into incorrect/partial/full categories, finding that performance remained high but lower than dichotomous items (accuracy ≈98% and F1 ≈0.977 for ME62300). This indicates that CNN-based validation is feasible for more complex graphical items with additional score categories, but operational deployment should expect reduced reliability for partial-credit distinctions and may require targeted data cleaning and augmentation.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS (all eight selected graphical response items; IRT-informed cleaning stage)
main_findings.target_variable: Identification of incorrectly or inconsistently scored responses (human rater vs IRT-expected-score agreement; CNN-assisted cleaning)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Data cleaning stage: CNN-human agreement increased after removing responses flagged as incorrectly or inconsistently scored; in Stage 2 (IRT-based ES), best models reached over 99% revised accuracy for dichotomous items (99.47%–99.92%) and 98.07% for the trichotomous item (Table 6). The study reports that CNNs helped identify up to ~2% of student responses as incorrectly or inconsistently scored by human raters (Conclusion).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical response item the study leveraged CNN-based automated scoring combined with IRT-based expected-score modeling to clean the training data and flag responses with potential human rater errors or inconsistencies, finding that revised agreement exceeded 99% for dichotomous items and about 98% for the trichotomous item after removing flagged cases. This indicates that CNNs can operationally function as a validation/quality-control layer in ILSA scoring workflows, enabling targeted re-scoring by content experts rather than full double-scoring, though the approach depends on manual review capacity and does not by itself establish causal scoring validity.

data.outcome_summary: This study evaluates whether convolutional neural networks can automatically score TIMSS 2019 eTIMSS graphical constructed-response items by matching human rater classifications. The authors selected eight items (five Grade 4 and three Grade 8; one Grade 8 item, ME62300, is trichotomous) and pre-processed student screenshots into fixed-size greyscale images for CNN training. Performance was assessed using hold-out validation and five-fold cross-validation, reporting exact-match accuracy, loss, and F1-scores to account for class imbalance. For the seven dichotomous items, best CNNs achieved very high agreement (average accuracy about 99.37%–99.92% and F1 between 0.9948 and 0.9992). For the trichotomous item ME62300, accuracy was 97.99% with F1 = 0.9766, and performance dropped on responses that were incorrectly human-scored (accuracy 88.81%). The paper does not report survey-weight usage or a missing-data strategy, so results should be interpreted as scoring-agreement validation rather than population-representative achievement estimation.
